title: Numbers 0-100 (Die Zahlen)
summary: Count, understand prices and phone numbers, and learn the one German number trick: 21 is 'one-and-twenty'.

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1, chapter 2: Contact details (Zahlen von 1 bis 100)

sections.title: 13 to 19
sections.text:
From 13 to 19 you say the number and then [[zehn]]: [[dreizehn]], [[vierzehn]], [[fünfzehn]], [[achtzehn]], [[neunzehn]].

Two of them lose letters: [[sechzehn]] (16, not 'sechs-zehn') and [[siebzehn]] (17, not 'sieben-zehn').

sections.title: The German number trick
sections.text:
From 21 on, German says the ones **first**, then the tens, joined with [[und]] (and), all in one word:

- 21 = [[einundzwanzig]] (one-and-twenty; [[eins]] loses its s here)
- 35 = [[fünfunddreißig]] (five-and-thirty)
- 99 = [[neunundneunzig]] (nine-and-ninety)

When you listen, wait for the end of the word: in [[siebenundvierzig]] the tens (40) come last.

Russian двадцать один and Armenian քսանմեկ both say the tens first; German says them last. Even English used to do this ('four-and-twenty blackbirds'). This needs practice with your ears, not your head, so do the listening exercises more than once.

sections.title: Phone numbers and prices
sections.text:
Phone numbers are usually read digit by digit or in pairs. The Munich area code 089 is [[null, acht, neun]]. On the phone people often say [[zwo]] instead of [[zwei]], so it doesn't sound like [[drei]].

Prices: [[zwei Euro fünfzig]] is 2,50 € (Germany writes a comma, not a point). The cents come after the word [[Euro]]. In a shop you hear [[Das kostet zwei Euro fünfzig.]] (That costs 2,50 €.)

items.question: Which number did you hear?
items.explanation: sieben-und-vierzig: 7 and 40, so 47. Listen for the end of the word.

items.question: Which number did you hear?
items.explanation: -zehn means 13 to 19; -zig means the tens. sechzehn = 16, sechzig = 60.

items.instruction: Listen and write the number as a word.
